subject: english
objective: Identify the claim, evidence, reasoning, counterclaim, and rebuttal in a persuasive (argument) paragraph; tell an arguable claim from a fact, a personal taste, or a vague statement; choose relevant, specific, credible evidence over weak evidence (bandwagon, single anecdote, biased or celebrity source, off-topic, opinion); choose reasoning that explains how evidence supports a claim; choose a fair counterclaim and a rebuttal that answers it with a reason; and write a paragraph that contains all five parts.
prerequisites: Can read and write a multi-sentence paragraph
Knows the difference between a fact and an opinion
standardsNote: None attached. Candidate alignments (for example Oklahoma Academic Standards for English Language Arts, or Common Core ELA W.6.1, W.7.1, and W.8.1 in states that use them) must be verified by the teacher before they are added.
sources: National Governors Association Center for Best Practices and Council of Chief State School Officers (2010). Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts, Appendix A, section 'Definitions of the Standards' Three Text Types', on argument versus persuasion (http://www.corestandards.org/assets/Appendix_A.pdf)
Toulmin, S. E. (1958; updated ed. 2003). The Uses of Argument. Cambridge University Press. Source of the claim, data (evidence), and warrant (reasoning) model, plus rebuttal.

McNeill, K. L., & Krajcik, J. (2012). Supporting Grade 5–8 Students in Constructing Explanations in Science: The Claim, Evidence, and Reasoning Framework for Talk and Writing. Pearson. Source of the claim–evidence–reasoning (CER) framing used here.
Purdue Online Writing Lab, Argumentative Essays (https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/academic_writing/essay_writing/argumentative_essays.html)
The Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Argument handout (https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/argument/)

Adolescent Sleep Working Group, Committee on Adolescence, and Council on School Health, American Academy of Pediatrics (2014). School Start Times for Adolescents. Pediatrics 134(3): 642–649 (https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2014-1697). The only real-world fact quoted in the lesson.
misconceptions: Any opinion is a claim, or a fact can serve as the claim
A louder or more emphatic claim is a stronger claim
More evidence is always better, and anything that sounds convincing counts as evidence
'Everyone knows' or a famous person's view is evidence
One vivid story proves what usually happens
Evidence speaks for itself, so reasoning just repeats the evidence or the claim
Mentioning the other side weakens your argument
A rebuttal means saying the other side is wrong or criticizing the people who hold it
Admitting any part of a counterclaim means giving up the argument
The claim must always be the first sentence
modelLimitations: Ridgeview Middle School and all of its people, surveys, and numbers are invented for practice; the lesson says so on screen. The only real-world fact is the 2014 American Academy of Pediatrics start-time recommendation.
Real persuasive writing has more parts (hooks, transitions, conclusions) and more than one reason; the lesson focuses on the five parts of one body paragraph.
Labels in 'Spot the parts' are one sentence per part. In real writing, one sentence can do two jobs, and reasoning can run across several sentences.
Evidence cards are sorted strong or weak for this claim. In real arguments strength is a matter of degree and depends on what the reasoning does with the evidence.

The checks in 'Build your own' look only for surface features (length, linking words such as 'because' and 'however', and a short list of insulting words). They cannot judge whether an argument is convincing, and the lesson says they are not a grade.
Nothing students write is saved or sent anywhere; the paragraph disappears when the page closes unless the student copies it.
The lesson uses the terms claim, evidence, reasoning, counterclaim, and rebuttal. Some curricula say reasons, warrant, opposing claim, or refutation instead.
